name: Pan-Africanism
summary: Pan-Africanism holds that Africans and people of African descent form one people with a common cause: ending colonial rule, racism and neo-colonial control, winning self-government for African peoples, and uniting the continent politically. The Pan-African Congresses (1900-1945), Nkrumah's call for a union government, the OAU and the African Union state this cause; its economics and domestic politics vary by strand, and its documents say little on social and moral questions.
scope: The doctrine on the African national question: self-determination, colonialism and neo-colonialism, sovereignty and borders, continental union, race and equality, the diaspora, culture, and the means of liberation. Based on the Pan-African Congress documents (Du Bois, 1919-1927; Manchester 1945), Nkrumah's writings and speeches, Garvey's Philosophy and Opinions, the OAU Charter, the Constitutive Act and Agenda 2063. Full programmes of Nkrumah's Ghana, the AU or any party (economy, welfare, social policy) are not taken as the doctrine; economic answers rest only on demands the Congress resolutions themselves state, and Nkrumah's socialism and one-party state are left unanswered as one strand's programme. Garveyite emigrationism is used only where it is shown to differ or agree.

notes: Searched all themes in the Congress documents, Nkrumah's books and speeches, Garvey, the OAU Charter, Constitutive Act and Agenda 2063; positions exist chiefly on self-determination, colonialism, borders and union, race and rights, the diaspora, culture, means, and the economic demands of the 1945 resolutions. Strands differ on borders (Manchester against the OAU/AU respect for colonial borders), on staying or emigrating (Du Bois's NAACP line against Garvey) and on means (Du Bois's 1921 Congress contemplated no force; the 1945 Congress and Nkrumah accepted armed struggle). Nkrumah's one-party state and socialism, Garvey's views on racial purity and the AU's gender-equality and market programme were not counted as the doctrine; they stay null. Several economic and social answers rest on regional resolutions (West Indies, East Africa) that the Fifth Congress adopted and so carry medium confidence at most. The 1919 Du Bois memorandum's tutelage language shows early Congresses softer than later ones.
